Me and my wife have to pay over 1500 bucks for an mri on her shoulder after insurance, but they can do it to this fruit for kicks? This is mildly infuriating for me.

The MRI costs relatively little in maintenance and electricity. You're paying for the operator. What's telling to me is that they don't book these things 24/7 like the first computers, when grad students got a chance to run their programs from 1 am to 5 am. Nah, there's plenty of machines and operators. Scheduling is done by convenience. What does it really cost? Look elsewhere: The Philippines straight up bills people about 6400 peso. About $150.

Of course, an American operator cost more than a Filipino. So, you can bump that up to... $200? The American MRI jockey is not making more than $50. But you do get to help recoup the hospitals costs of the three people who didn't pay and the adminstration fees of tracking them down and the several levels of administration in the hospital and the insurance company. You're helping keep a lot of people employed.

The banana? He didn't owe them shit.

Yeah a lot of the cost of an MRI is the trained operator, but moreso MRIs are expensive, complex machines that require liquid helium to operate. They aren't cheap, and someone's gotta pay for the amortized cost of capital equipment.

And how is that not true in the Philippines?

Liquid helium is not cheap, but neither is it so prohibitively expensive that 80% of the posters haven't frozen a rose or balloon or seen some equally wasteful demonstration. An MRI machine can be as cheap as $150k or up to $3m for a custom build. A new one is a little over a million.

Back to the shoulder example: Take $250 for the operator (too high by a factor of 5). Take $250 for the liquid helium (equally absurd). That leaves $1000 for the shoulder. Figure the time on the machine takes an hour. Taking a little lunch, figure that there are 5 scans a day. Assume a 5 day week. (Neither of which would we do if the amortized capital was really an issue.) At $25,000 a week, in one year the machine is completely paid off an profitable.

There are associated costs (overhead in housing it, blah, blah), but I don't believe your counter argument. There's a LOT of highballing in that estimate. Try googling the cost of liquid helium, for example. You're paying for administration.

The costs are adjusted for medical insurance. Insurance companies will not pay $1500, instead they'll say how much it's worth and pay the hospital X amount. When Joe Average comes in and gets slapped with a $1500 bill and has no insurance, he'll take it at face value. What he should do instead is talk directly to the hospital about it, and get an actual reasonable price. Well, as reasonable as it can get anyway.
